analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on oil and chemical companies to fund toxic-waste site cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program cleans up the nation's worst toxic-waste sites, and for years it was paid for by the companies that created the pollution, through taxes on crude oil, petroleum products, and chemicals, plus a special corporate environmental income tax. Those taxes expired at the end of 1995, shifting the cleanup bill onto ordinary taxpayers through general revenue. This bill would have brought those polluter-pays taxes back from enactment through 2008, and extended a related tax on diesel that pays for cleaning leaking underground storage tanks.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently fund Superfund cleanups through general revenue instead of the polluters; and communities near hazardous-waste sites, which would benefit from a better-funded cleanup program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: General taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate and the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund financing rate, both through October 1, 2008, so cleanup funding again comes from petroleum and chemical taxes rather than general revenue.

Reinstates the Corporate Environmental Income Tax on corporations through taxable years beginning before January 1, 2008, restoring a dedicated revenue source tied to the corporations the program regulates.
Extends the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund financing rate (a diesel tax) until October 1, 2008, to keep paying for cleanups of petroleum leaks from storage tanks.

analysis.who_pays: Petroleum companies, importers, and refiners, which pay the per-barrel crude oil and petroleum product taxes; chemical and other large corporations, which pay the corporate environmental income tax; the tax burden is typically passed at least partly into fuel and product prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, petroleum, and large chemical corporations

drawbacks.text: The excise taxes are levied on crude oil and petroleum products received at refineries, and companies commonly pass such costs into fuel prices, so consumers would pay slightly more at the pump.

The corporate environmental income tax applies to large corporations based on alternative minimum taxable income, and industry groups have long argued such taxes raise production costs without being directly tied to a company's actual pollution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but slow-moving: restoring polluter-pays funding means toxic-site cleanups stop drawing entirely on general taxpayer money, at the modest cost of small price increases for oil products. The bill does nothing to speed up cleanups themselves, so its main effect is who pays, not how fast sites are fixed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on February 5, 2003.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax bills.
Five Democrats joined as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored it.
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, petroleum, and chemical companies were better off, since the polluter-pays taxes were never reinstated and Superfund cleanups continued to be financed by general taxpayers instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies; general taxpayers keep paying

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the Superfund, Oil Spill Liability, and Leaking Underground Storage Tank taxes.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration opposed reinstating the Superfund excise taxes, and the taxes remained lapsed throughout his term.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, so no roll-call exists; the record shows all six sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never acted.

industries.note: The bill reinstates per-barrel taxes on crude oil and petroleum products received at refineries, a direct cost to the industry. Its interest in avoiding the tax runs against the public's interest in shifting Superfund cleanup costs off general taxpayers.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and other large corporations
industries.note: The corporate environmental income tax would apply again to large corporations, restoring a tax that expired in 1995. Avoiding it while cleanup costs fall on general taxpayers is the industry's interest here.
Since the taxes expired in 1995, Superfund cleanups have been paid from general revenue; the bill would relieve that burden but add small costs into fuel prices.
